Hmm interesting, I guess even msys binutils doesnt allow for whatever link arg `#[linkage = "weak"]` ends up emitting then (which doesn't give me much hope for msvc either). Not too surprising. What would really be nice is to solve this at a library level instead of having a big document of "you need to do XY and Z in your crate for this to work" so if we can get it working in qemu-plugin's build rs that would be ideal (and if we can come up with something for Linux/macos which doesn't need nightly that would be nice too.
Wow, this is awesome, quite a productive holiday season 😉 I'll take a look!

I had a couple of ideas about the g_free problem, but haven't had a chance to try them yet.

1. Try and resolve the g_free relative virtual address by inspecting the qemu binary, add that to the base address that qemu is loaded at and cast it to a fptr and use that. Not sure if I'll be able to do this, will require sufficient debug info in qemu.
2. I think that on windows glib ends up just calling the 'normal' free function you get from Windows. If so, we might get away with calling that directly. If this worked, we would be relying on glib never changing internal details of his it mallocs and frees on windows.
Good enough for me, IMO better to make it work now than stress too much about it breaking in the future! Thanks for testing this out!

I know combining "fix CI" and "add a feature" in one PR is bad practice, but luckily this repo has 5 stars so I think I can get away with it for now. I'll merge this once I can get CI to work, I just checked and there's enough space so something else weird is going on. The built image is 30.2GB, well under the available space.

Actually, maybe it should be kept -- there is no qemu-user on Windows so ostensibly we'll want to test things when running programs at some point. This will need to be done with a plugin that can be dynamically toggled somehow, obviously, because we don't want to be booting with a plugin that dumps full disas.
Confirmed locally that `cargo build -r -p qemu` builds 8.1.2.

I think that would repair the behavior to be how you intended it as well as remove some confusion (at least for me, a windows noob).

I don't know how to fix the failing windows build.
Looks like windows is failing (it still is, just there's no asserts) because plugin api version has changed: https://github.com/qemu/qemu/commit/926e146eff8d7b89754e8b681f80e962d220f077

Hmm. Hard to know how to fix - qemu now only supports plugin version 2 or higher. But if you wanted to compile a plugin for an older qemu, you'd want to specify version 1 in the plugin you're building. Feature gate it? or maybe keep multilple versions of the API around and let the user declare/use the correct one? maybe const generics?
It was qemu version 9.0.0 that first requires plugin api v2. prior to that (8.2.4) it is v1, and everything is fine. I'll open a separate issue (#15).
Note also that qemu 9.0.0/plugin version 2 includes plugin functions to read register state. It also adds a `#include <glib.h>` to the header, which generate-bindings will have to handle...

A couple odds and ends not in here yet:

- Update documentation about the plugin API version now being feature-flag-controlled (`plugin-api-vX`)
- Add a convenience function for compiling a plugin thrice for each version? Maybe not necessary.

Update: the problem appears when building natively using all available threads of the cpu in the 13th gen architecture.
Running the build in a single threaded way solves the problem.
Multicore build is fine on older intel architectures apparently - no problem with kaby lake.
Thanks for the report and for figuring out what's going on, maybe the build should default to single core unless specified...

Hmm, I think your diagnosis is correct. The issue is that we just link as extern for these symbols, and Unicorn's static blob happens to provide them just how we asked for them (and this static linkage is prioritized over dynamic linkage). This is pretty unfortunate, but it makes sense. It's possible that having a `#[link(name = "...", kind = "dylib")]` would help,but I'm not sure if it would compile with a wrong (or unknown at compile time) name.

You may also like to try building with `-Cprefer-dynamic`. I'm not sure if it will do anything but it's probably worth a try :)

Interesting, that's good to know. I wonder if I can get unicorn to statically link glib in if this wouldn't 'fix' it. I think this is more something I'd have to do with unicorn, though, since QEMU is the consumer and not the library.

Hmm, I don't like this solution because someone pulling in this crate from crates.io will encounter errors and it'll be very unclear why. I agree the weak linking isn't ideal, but removing it is worse IMO without a suitable replacement. If you'd like to come up with something, feel free, and if it really is broken on MacOS, we can disable it there, but let's leave it in for Linux for the time being while we think of a true solution.

> Hmm, I don't like this solution because someone pulling in this crate from crates.io will encounter errors and it'll be very unclear why.

That makes sense, looking for the cleanest user experience is important.  (For what it's worth: the status quo with `unix-weak-link` wasn't great on this front even before I hit the macOS issue.  The docs didn't mention that it was necessary or that undefined symbols were expected without it.  It took some sleuthing through the code and CI tests to figure it out.)

> I agree the weak linking isn't ideal, but removing it is worse IMO without a suitable replacement. If you'd like to come up with something, feel free, and if it really is broken on MacOS, we can disable it there, but let's leave it in for Linux for the time being while we think of a true solution.

I think #30 fits the bill here.  Adding those options to qemu-plugin-sys's build.rs fixes the issue for my downstream, cdylib plugin without needing the `unix-weak-link` feature or any ".cargo/config.toml".  The options just appear to be propagated to the linker as hoped. (I tested on x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux, and aarch64-darwin.)
Ok this is great! I will test this as soon as I have a minute. I really appreciate the time you spent to look for a nice way to do this, thank you :)
I like this idea but would it be better to just implement `std::io::Read`?

> I like this idea but would it be better to just implement `std::io::Read`?

Happy to do either way. (For my purposes I’m filling a 2-byte array so it won’t make a difference.) I can give a `Read` implementation a go soon.

> I like this idea but would it be better to just implement `std::io::Read`?

Ah, digging into this it is (a little) uglier: since `Read` acts like a cursor there's a need to track state (the position) and either buffer internally or (on subsequent `read()`s) re-read each time to a scratch buffer then copy the bytes starting at the cursor's current offset.

I think that juice probably isn't worth the squeeze?  (Maybe I'm missing something though, always happy to hear thoughts?)
Ahh I forgot about that. This is fine for me then :)

Contrary to C++ `qemu-plugin` fares rather well as as an external code-base targeting the C API. And as long as QEMU does not go full Rust a "native" plugin API does not offer a real advantage: a translation layer of some sort is always required for a safe/high-level API and that layer may as well live outside the QEMU tree. However, having `qemu-plugin-sys` maintained as part of QEMU would certainly simplify keeping up with changes. That obviously means more to care about as a QEMU maintainer, particularly around releases, but you are already aware of that.

In any case, we do want "bare" bindings (e.g. `qemu-plugin-sys`) and higher level API (`qemu-plugin`) to be available via crates.io as separate crates. Whether both come from the same place or not is not that important imo. I would volunteer to continue development wherever we decide to host things in the end.

In a discussion on qemu-devel years(?) ago I stated that you can have very light-weight callbacks without the need to dispatch on boxed fat pointers. `qemu-plugin-rs` is doing the latter in at least places and I was meaning to submit changes tackling that, but failed to allocate time to actually do so. There are some other aspects that do require possibly costly (and ugly) abstractions such as glib types (`GArray`, `GByteArray`) and per-CPU state keeping (which requires locking for the state itself as well as a separate map behind a mutex and/or stuffing pointers into a scoreboard), but that's nothing completely unmanageable.

IIUC `qemu-plugin` does not current free any of the data it ought to on TB cache flushes. IMO a high level API should register a callback for that using `qemu_plugin_register_flush_cb`, but `qemu-plugin` does not. It just exposes that fn. Another thing I meant to rectify at some point.

You're right, and a major flaw in what I posted above. If we are really forced to have an allocation per callback, then we should probably keep the current approach of `qemu-rs`, which allows closures with captures.

The only other approach that comes to my mind would be to express (I think we can't) that the lifetime of userdata is always greater or equal than the one of a surrounding callback. But even if we could express that, we would end up having static lifetimes everywhere, which would be useless.
